choices.text: The branch of chemistry concerned with the three-dimensional aspects of molecules
The study of which atoms are bonded to which in a molecule
choices.why: The order of connection is what distinguishes constitutional isomers. Stereochemistry adds the third dimension: how the atoms are arranged in space.

choices.text: The study of the energy released when molecules burn
choices.why: That is combustion. Stereochemistry deals with the spatial arrangement of atoms.

choices.text: The branch of chemistry that draws molecules in two dimensions
choices.why: Stereochemistry is exactly the step beyond a two-dimensional view.

explanation: Stereochemistry is the branch of chemistry concerned with the three-dimensional aspects of molecules. A molecule's exact three-dimensional structure is often crucial to its properties and biological behavior.

prompt: Why is rotation possible around the carbon–carbon single bond in ethane?

choices.text: The σ bond is cylindrically symmetrical, so rotating it does not change the orbital overlap
The C–C bond is a π bond, which is free to twist
choices.why: A C–C single bond is a σ bond. Its cylindrical symmetry is what allows rotation.

choices.text: The bond breaks and re-forms as the carbons turn
choices.why: No bond breaks; a cross-section of the σ bond is a circle, so the overlap is the same at every angle.

choices.text: The hydrogens repel each other strongly enough to push the carbons around
choices.why: Rotation is possible because of the σ bond's symmetry, not because the hydrogens drive it.

explanation: σ bonds are cylindrically symmetrical: a plane cutting through a carbon–carbon single-bond orbital looks like a circle. Because of this symmetry, rotation is possible around carbon–carbon bonds in open-chain molecules (Figure 3.6.1).

choices.text: Molecules that differ only in the arrangement of atoms produced by rotation around single bonds
Compounds with the same formula but atoms connected in a different order
choices.why: Those are constitutional isomers. Conformers have the same connections and differ only by bond rotation.

choices.text: Molecules that differ in the number of hydrogens
choices.why: Conformers are the same molecule with a different spatial arrangement, so the formula is identical.

choices.text: Different drawings, such as sawhorse and Newman, of the same arrangement
choices.why: Those are representations. Conformers are actually different arrangements of the atoms.

explanation: The different arrangements of atoms that result from bond rotation are called conformations, and molecules that have different arrangements are called conformational isomers, or conformers.

prompt: Unlike constitutional isomers, different conformers usually can't be isolated. Why?

choices.text: They interconvert too rapidly
They are identical in every respect, so there is nothing to separate
choices.why: Conformers differ in arrangement and in energy; they just turn into one another too fast to separate.

choices.text: Isolating one would require breaking a covalent bond
choices.why: Interconversion needs only rotation around a single bond, which is why it is so fast.

choices.text: Only one conformer exists at any temperature
choices.why: All conformers are present together, interconverting rapidly.

explanation: Different conformers often can't be isolated because they interconvert too rapidly, by rotation around σ bonds.

prompt: In a Newman projection, how are the bonds to the rear carbon drawn?

choices.text: As lines to the edge of the circle
As lines to the center of the circle
choices.why: Lines to the center are the bonds of the front carbon.

choices.text: As wedges pointing out of the page
choices.why: A Newman projection uses a circle for the carbons: front-carbon bonds go to the center and rear-carbon bonds to the edge.

choices.text: They are not shown, since the front carbon hides them
choices.why: All six bonds are shown; the rear carbon's bonds start at the edge of the circle.

explanation: A Newman projection views the carbon–carbon bond end-on and represents the two carbon atoms by a circle. Bonds to the front carbon are lines to the center of the circle; bonds to the rear carbon are lines to the edge.

prompt: How does a sawhorse representation differ from a Newman projection?

choices.text: A sawhorse views the C–C bond from an oblique angle; a Newman projection views it end-on
A sawhorse views the C–C bond end-on; a Newman projection views it from the side
choices.why: It is the other way around: the Newman projection is the end-on view, with the two carbons as one circle.

choices.text: A sawhorse leaves out the C–H bonds
choices.why: A sawhorse shows all the C–H bonds to indicate spatial orientation.

choices.text: Only a sawhorse can show conformations
choices.why: Both are ways of representing conformational isomers (Figure 3.6.2).

explanation: A sawhorse representation views the carbon–carbon bond from an oblique angle and shows all C–H bonds. A Newman projection views the carbon–carbon bond directly end-on and represents the two carbons by a circle (Figure 3.6.2).

prompt: How large is the barrier to rotation around the C–C bond in ethane, in kJ/mol?
explanation: Experiments show a small barrier of 12 kJ/mol (2.9 kcal/mol). The staggered conformations are 12 kJ/mol lower in energy than the eclipsed ones (Figure 3.6.3).

prompt: Which statement about rotation around the C–C bond in ethane is correct?

choices.text: Rotation happens, but a small barrier makes some conformations more stable than others
Rotation is perfectly free: every conformation has the same energy
choices.why: Experiments show a 12 kJ/mol barrier, so rotation is not perfectly free.

choices.text: No rotation is possible around a single bond
choices.why: The σ bond's cylindrical symmetry allows rotation; ethane's hydrogens constantly change their relative positions.

choices.text: The barrier is so high that ethane is locked in one conformation
choices.why: The barrier is small, 12 kJ/mol, and the conformations interconvert rapidly.

explanation: We don't observe perfectly free rotation in ethane. There is a small (12 kJ/mol) barrier to rotation, and some conformations are more stable than others.

prompt: Which conformation of ethane is the most stable?

choices.text: Staggered, with the six C–H bonds as far from one another as possible
Eclipsed, with the six C–H bonds as close as possible
choices.why: The eclipsed conformation is the highest-energy, least stable one.

choices.text: All conformations are equally stable
choices.why: The eclipsed conformation is 12 kJ/mol higher in energy than the staggered one.

choices.text: One halfway between staggered and eclipsed
choices.why: Energy minima occur exactly at the staggered conformations (Figure 3.6.3).

explanation: The lowest-energy, most stable conformation is the one in which all six C–H bonds are as far away from one another as possible: staggered when viewed end-on in a Newman projection.

prompt: At any given instant, about what percentage of ethane molecules have an approximately staggered conformation?
explanation: About 99% of ethane molecules have an approximately staggered conformation at any instant, and only about 1% are near the eclipsed conformation.

prompt: What is torsional strain in ethane?

choices.text: The extra energy of the eclipsed conformation compared with the staggered one
The energy needed to break the C–C bond
choices.why: No bond breaks in rotation. Torsional strain is the 12 kJ/mol extra energy of the eclipsed conformation.

choices.text: The extra energy of the staggered conformation compared with the eclipsed one
choices.why: The staggered conformation is the lower-energy one; the eclipsed conformation carries the strain.

choices.text: The strain from bending the H–C–H bond angles away from 109.5°
choices.why: Torsional strain comes from eclipsing bonds on adjacent carbons, not from distorted bond angles.

explanation: The extra 12 kJ/mol of energy present in the eclipsed conformation of ethane is called torsional strain.

prompt: What is the major factor behind torsional strain in ethane?

choices.text: An interaction between C–H bonding orbitals on one carbon and antibonding orbitals on the adjacent carbon, which stabilizes the staggered conformation
The hydrogen atoms bumping into each other in the eclipsed conformation
choices.why: Crowding of atoms is not the main cause here. The major factor in ethane is an orbital interaction that stabilizes the staggered conformation.

choices.text: Bending of the C–C bond in the eclipsed conformation
choices.why: The C–C bond is not bent; the strain comes from how the C–H orbitals on adjacent carbons interact.

choices.text: Breaking of the σ bond's overlap during rotation
choices.why: The σ bond is cylindrically symmetrical, so its overlap does not change with rotation.

explanation: The cause of torsional strain has been the subject of controversy, but the major factor is an interaction between C–H bonding orbitals on one carbon and antibonding orbitals on the adjacent carbon, which stabilizes the staggered conformation relative to the eclipsed one.

prompt: How many hydrogen–hydrogen eclipsing interactions are there in the eclipsed conformation of ethane?
explanation: Each of the three C–H bonds on the front carbon eclipses one C–H bond on the rear carbon, giving three equal H–H eclipsing interactions that together make up the 12 kJ/mol of torsional strain.

prompt: What energy cost is assigned to a single H–H eclipsing interaction, in kJ/mol?
explanation: The total strain of 12 kJ/mol arises from three equal hydrogen–hydrogen eclipsing interactions, so each is assigned 12 ÷ 3 = 4.0 kJ/mol (1.0 kcal/mol).

prompt: Starting from a staggered conformation of ethane, through how many degrees must the rear carbon rotate to reach an eclipsed conformation?
explanation: Rotating the rear carbon of staggered ethane by 60° brings its C–H bonds directly behind those of the front carbon, giving the eclipsed conformation.

prompt: What is the dihedral angle in a Newman projection of ethane?

choices.text: The angle between C–H bonds on the front and back carbons, viewed end-on
The H–C–H bond angle on one carbon
choices.why: That is a bond angle within one carbon. The dihedral angle compares bonds on the two different carbons.

choices.text: The H–C–C bond angle
choices.why: That angle stays about the same during rotation. The dihedral angle is the one that changes as the C–C bond rotates.

choices.text: The angle at which the C–C bond is viewed in a sawhorse drawing
choices.why: That is the oblique viewing angle of the drawing, not a property of the molecule.

explanation: The dihedral angle is the angle between C–H bonds on the front and back carbons as viewed end-on. On a graph of potential energy versus rotation it goes full circle from 0 to 360°, with minima at staggered and maxima at eclipsed conformations (Figure 3.6.3).

prompt: How many energy maxima does ethane pass through during one full 360° rotation around its C–C bond?
explanation: Energy maxima occur at eclipsed conformations. Each 60° rotation switches between staggered and eclipsed, so eclipsed conformations come every 120°: three maxima (and three staggered minima) in 360°.
